sentences.text: Itasuchus featured a long, flattened snout equipped with interlocking teeth similar to those of modern crocodilians.
The animal was protected by thick bony armor plates that might have been overlain by a soft, leathery skin layer.
Estimates suggest the skull measured roughly 37 centimeters in length, while the lower jaw could extend up to 43 centimeters.
Air intake occurred through nostrils positioned near the snout tip, opening both forward and upward.
The upper jaw bones likely held five teeth each, with the third tooth being the largest in the row.
The lower jaw contained approximately 18 teeth, although two were absent from the primary specimen used for description.
Small, deep pits on the armor surface sometimes formed channels that radiated outward from a central ridge.
A known skull measuring 370 millimeters long implies a total body length of about three meters.
Among its relatives, Itasuchus was likely the heaviest individual due to its exceptionally thick armor.
The vast surface area of its armor plates likely allowed the animal to absorb heat quickly and become active rapidly.
The genus was first formally described by Price in 1955.
Llewellyn Ivor Price named the creature based on fossils discovered near Peirópolis.
The type species, Itasuchus jesuinoi, was described from Maastrichtian-aged rocks in the Marília Formation of Uberaba, Brazil.
The initial scientific description relied primarily on cranial remains.
Fossils of the type species were originally found in the Serra da Galga Formation.
Subsequent discoveries support the presence of the genus in the Presidente Prudente Formation.
By 2018, a second specimen, cataloged as MUGEO 218-V, was assigned to the genus at the generic level only.
Scientists interpret Itasuchus as a semi-aquatic animal.
The presence of osteoderms is cited as evidence supporting this semi-aquatic lifestyle.
A laterally flattened tail and keeled armor plates may have helped make the animal more hydrodynamic.
Marinho and colleagues argue that the keels on the armor made the creature hydrodynamic and stable when submerged.
The flattened tail and shifted keels effectively created a paddle for swimming.
Marinho and colleagues hypothesize that the heavy armor made moving on land difficult for Itasuchus.
The genus Itasuchus was established by Price in 1955.
In 2004, Carvalho and colleagues coined the family Itasuchidae to unite Itasuchus with Malawisuchus.
The family Itasuchidae was established in 2004 to include Itasuchus and Malawisuchus.
The clade name Itasuchidae was revived in 2018 by Pinheiro and colleagues.
Pinheiro and colleagues redefined the clade Itasuchidae in 2018 to include other similar forms.
The Paleobi Database lists Itasuchus as belonging to the parent group Itasuchidae.
A 2023 analysis placed Itasuchus close to the brevirostrine peirosaurid Antaeusuchus.
The placement of Itasuchus in Trematochampsidae is debated due to potential issues with the holotype of Trematochampsa.
The family classification of Itasuchus is debated, with Trematochampsidae being a proposed but uncertain family.
It is debated whether Caririsuchus camposi should be classified as a species of Itasuchus, a proposal made by Buffetaut that was not widely accepted.
Itasuchus lived from the Campanian to the Maastrichtian, between 83.6 and 66 million years ago.
The animal inhabited river systems during the late Campanian and early Maastrichtian stages.
The environment where Itasuchus lived likely had an arid to semi-arid climate that experienced wetter periods.
